content: The ABO blood group system is a classification method used to identify the presence or absence of A and B antigens on the surface of red blood cells (erythrocytes). It is the most clinically significant of the 36 recognized blood group systems in human medicine, particularly in the context of blood transfusions. A mismatch in the ABO system, or any other blood group system, can lead to severe and potentially fatal immune reactions during transfusions or organ transplants. The antibodies associated with the ABO system, anti-A and anti-B, are typically of the IgM class and are produced early in life due to exposure to environmental antigens such as food, bacteria, and viruses. The ABO blood group system was discovered in 1901 by Karl Landsteiner, an Austrian physician, who later received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1930 for this groundbreaking work. Landsteiner observed that blood from different individuals could agglutinate (clump together) when mixed, and he classified human blood into three groups: A, B, and C (later renamed O). He also identified two antigens, A and B, and their corresponding antibodies, anti-A and anti-B. His students later discovered a fourth group, AB. The genetic inheritance of these blood groups was explained in 1910 by Ludwik Hirszfeld and Emil von Dungern, who introduced the terms O and AB. The modern classification system using the letters A, B, AB, and O was universally adopted by the 1950s. The ABO blood group is determined by a single gene, the ABO gene, located on chromosome 9q34. This gene encodes a glycosyltransferase enzyme that modifies the carbohydrate structures on red blood cell antigens. There are three main alleles: IA, IB, and i. The IA allele produces type A blood, IB produces type B blood, and i produces type O blood. Both IA and IB are dominant over i, and individuals with IAIB exhibit codominance, expressing both A and B antigens. Rare phenotypes, such as cis-AB, result from a single enzyme that synthesizes both A and B antigens. The distribution of ABO blood groups varies globally and within populations, influenced by evolutionary and migratory patterns. The O allele is thought to have ancient origins, predating human migration out of Africa. Evolutionary theories suggest that the diversity of ABO alleles is maintained by balancing selection, where individuals with rare blood types may have an advantage in recognizing pathogens. ABO antigens are not only present on red blood cells but also on epithelial cells and other tissues. They play roles in cell membrane integrity, adhesion, and acting as receptors for extracellular molecules. The ABO system also influences the von Willebrand factor (vWF), a glycoprotein involved in hemostasis. Individuals with type O blood have lower levels of vWF and are more prone to bleeding, while non-O individuals have higher vWF levels and an increased risk of thrombotic events. The ABO blood group is associated with various disease risks. For example, type O blood is linked to a reduced risk of pancreatic cancer but an increased susceptibility to severe cholera infections. Conversely, type A blood is associated with a higher risk of gastric cancer. These associations are thought to arise from interactions between blood group antigens and pathogens or other environmental factors. Incompatibilities in the ABO system can lead to hemolytic disease of the newborn (HDN), although this is rare because most ABO antibodies are IgM and do not cross the placenta. However, in type O mothers, IgG antibodies can cross the placenta and cause HDN in the fetus. Recent advancements in biotechnology have enabled the conversion of A, B, and AB blood into type O using glycosidase enzymes to remove antigens from red blood cells. This method, while promising, does not address the Rh antigen and requires further clinical trials. Artificial blood is also being explored as a potential solution to blood type compatibility issues. Despite its scientific basis, the ABO blood group system has been the subject of pseudoscientific claims, such as linking blood types to personality traits or dietary preferences. These ideas lack scientific evidence and remain unsupported by rigorous research.
